lesson.title: Proteins: Twenty Letters, an Unlimited Vocabulary of Function
lesson.summary: Proteins are polymers built from twenty different amino acid monomers linked by condensation reactions into peptide bonds, and the particular sequence and chemistry of those amino acids lets a single class of molecule act as enzyme, structural fiber, transporter, and messenger all at once.
lesson.body:
Proteins close out this survey of biological macromolecules, following the same monomer to polymer logic that carbohydrates and lipids already demonstrated, just with a far more chemically diverse monomer. The monomer of a protein is an amino acid, a small molecule built around a central carbon atom, called the alpha carbon, bonded to four different groups: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a single hydrogen atom, and a variable side chain known as the R group. There are twenty standard amino acids used across essentially all known life, and every one shares that identical amino and carboxyl backbone. What distinguishes one amino acid from another, and what ultimately gives proteins their staggering functional range, is entirely a matter of that variable R group, which can be as simple as a single hydrogen atom in glycine or as elaborate as a charged, ring containing side chain in arginine or tryptophan.

Those R groups fall into recognizable functional group categories: some are nonpolar hydrocarbon chains that avoid water, some carry polar hydroxyl or amide groups that interact favorably with water, and some carry fully charged acidic or basic groups. This spread of chemical personalities packed into twenty interchangeable building blocks is what makes proteins so much more versatile than carbohydrates, whose monomers differ mainly in ring size and stereochemistry rather than in fundamental chemistry.

Amino acids link together through the same condensation chemistry that builds every other biological polymer. The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, releasing a water molecule and forming a new covalent linkage called a peptide bond. A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds is called a polypeptide, and one or more folded polypeptide chains make up a finished protein. As with carbohydrates, this bond forming reaction is reversible: hydrolysis, catalyzed by protease enzymes, adds water back across a peptide bond and splits the chain apart, exactly how dietary protein is digested into amino acids the small intestine can absorb.

The sequence in which amino acids are strung together, a protein's primary structure, is dictated by the genetic code and determines everything about how the finished protein folds and behaves. Because different R groups attract or repel water, and each other, differently, a polypeptide chain spontaneously folds as it is made, first into local coiled or pleated patterns called secondary structure, then into an overall compact shape called tertiary structure, and sometimes assembling with other chains into a multi subunit quaternary structure. This folding is the entire basis of protein function, since a protein's precise shape determines what molecules it can bind and what chemistry it can carry out.

That functional range is enormous compared to what carbohydrates or lipids accomplish. Enzymes, proteins that catalyze reactions, include the amylase, lactase, and lipase molecules mentioned in earlier sections, each shaped precisely enough to recognize one specific glycosidic or ester bond. Structural proteins like collagen and keratin support skin, tendons, and hair. Transport proteins like hemoglobin carry oxygen through blood. Signaling proteins like insulin regulate blood glucose, tying this chapter together, since insulin is itself a protein whose job is controlling how cells take up and store the carbohydrate molecules this chapter began with.
